source_text: So, building the correspondence from 象 markup of my turns to the structured agent reply and then the *next* turn would be easier if I was using the same codes in my reply, e.g. "🈸:yes" would be very easy to code. Maybe we could add Emacs bindings for those symbols, or better yet a Hydra that includes keypresses and the short intent labels from CLAUDE.md.  As opposed to UI work, the computational challenge seems to be threading all of this through into a model of the session rather than just a model of a turn-by-turn verbal ping-pong match.  Here, again, I think we could get some inspiration from the War Machine work and maybe also contribute something back.  I.e. how does the War Machine make sense of incremental progress?  Maybe the difference is that the War Machine has a *little* room for emergent learning (I was just talking about this with codex-10), e.g., selecting a new pattern to get unstuck, whereas the Operator+Agent dialogues are very generative, e.g., the idea we are talking about now wasn't written down in any previous mission file.

reply_text:
Fixing a hydra docstring error in the new mark menu (C-c ;) before I reply.㊥ Gist: The mark menu is in place. In the Claude, Codex, Kimi and Zai REPLs, C-c ; opens a hydra listing each key, its mark and its intent, so pressing s inserts 🈸 and you type ":yes" after it. On the harder part, I'd model the session as a ledger of open items, not as turn-by-turn ping-pong. Each request or proposal stays open until a later turn or a commit closes it, and items that first appear in the dialogue get a "minted here" flag. That gives the War Machine a record of where new ideas came from, which it doesn't have now.

㊢ (the menu, commit 73bb40f7) It's loaded in your running Emacs now. I tested it there: pressing s, then typing ":yes", gave "🈸:yes".
- **Keys:** the letters follow the intent names where they can: p propose, a approve, d disagree, s ask-action, c clarify, n constrain, z defer, ! report-problem, and "." for unresolved. The menu shows the whole list.
- **Problem fixed:** a hydra hint has to start with a newline, or it fails when shown with "Not enough arguments for format string".

🈖 (session, not ping-pong) A reply to the turn before it is only the simplest case. A 🈸 from Tuesday can be settled by a commit on Wednesday, or dropped without anyone saying so. So I'd keep a ledger of open items:
- **Opened by:** an agent's ㊭ or 🈸, or yours.
- **Closed by:** a marked answer (🈸:yes), an approve or disagree that 象 reads, a commit that carries the turn's trailers, or a later 🈡 withdraw.
- **Still open at the end of a session:** the "no response" class the paper says is missing.

That's computable from what exists today. It also serves the pilot, since a team's requests left open are exactly what the audit reports.

🈖 (what the War Machine offers) As I understand it from what's recorded here, the War Machine counts progress against a fixed list. Each click must clear an unchecked checklist item. Open obligations go to the front of selection. A repair comes before the next click if that click would repeat the last failure. Its room for learning is choosing from patterns it already has, as you said, plus "mint missing fundamentals first" as a deliberate, rare step. The ledger can borrow the first two directly: items carried across turns, and open items surfacing before new ones.

㊭ (what dialogue could give back) The difference you point to is that dialogue mints items all the time. The idea we're discussing now wasn't in any mission file. So the ledger should flag any item whose text has no close match among mission files, earlier ledger items or patterns as "minted in session X, turn Y". Those flags would give the War Machine a supply of new candidate items, each traceable to the conversation that produced it, instead of minting being an exception it handles alone. Whether the flags are accurate enough to use would show in the first week of data. A simple text match will both miss rephrasings and over-flag.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I build the ledger v0 over this session and the last few days? Agent marks since 30 September and your turns as 象 reads them, with open, closed and minted counts, and a short list of minted items for you to judge by eye.

previous_reply_acts.text:
(what's written, `futon7/holes/M-futon-forward-model.demand-v0.edn`, commit 777490b) The file sits alongside the mission's existing backlog-and-market roadmap, which covers the supply side.
- **Segments (4):** team lead, engineering org, agent founder, and a heavy solo user like you.
- **Pains (6):**
  - dropped or repeated requests
  - token cost
  - lessons from sessions not becoming team rules (what XTrace sells)
  - production observability (crowded, so not ours)
  - uncurated memory
  - follow-through in the organisation: proposals unanswered, so nobody can tell a rejection from no response (the 108 unanswered proposals from the paper's WR-0)
- **Build-outs (5), marked by whether a demo exists:** fast mode does; the rollout audit and pattern memory partly do; the request audit and proposal recording don't.
- **Hypotheses (3):** each has a test, including yours about AIF.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (your point about clicks) I agree, and the model shows what follows for the site. A click on the 小象 demo shows interest in reading intent, not in any particular build-out. A click on a page that names one pain and one offer does tell us which pain. So the 小象 page should lead to one short offer page per pain, not a general contact link. That turns the website into a source of evidence for the model.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (AIF as the part behind the demo) Since yesterday, agent replies carry a mark on each paragraph, so a proposal (㊭) or a request for a decision (🈸) can be found by script. 象 and 小象 already read your next turn. Pairing the two gives, for each proposal: accepted, declined, or no response. That is the three-way record `sec-operator.tex` says is missing. With it, the agents' proposal policy can learn from your answers, which the AIF loop needs. You would get something useful straight away: a weekly count of what you accept and ignore, by kind of proposal. It is also what you could show people without explaining active inference.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (your hypothesis about XTrace and Tessl) I recorded it as hypothesis `:h/aif-gap`. Its test is one question you can ask at Tech Week: "Does the tool change what agents propose, based on what you accepted or declined?" I also wrote the condition you stated: it sells only once shown on your own record, with a before and after.
